label: Stoicism
title: What Is Truly in Your Control? – Epictetus and the Art of Inner Freedom
title_card: What Is Truly in Your Control?
thumbnail_text: What is truly in your control?
description: Nearly 2,000 years ago, Epictetus – a former slave who became one of the most influential Stoic teachers – answered one question with a single distinction: what is truly in our control? In this calm, story-driven essay we explore the dichotomy of control, why our judgments shape our emotions, the Stoic image of the archer, and how James Stockdale leaned on these ideas during years of captivity. At the end you'll find a simple exercise you can use today.

sections.text:
You are stuck in traffic. You are going to be late, and you can feel your heart beating faster. Your hands tighten on the wheel. You check the clock again, as if checking it could change anything.

Now ask yourself a simple question. Of everything happening in this moment, what is actually in your hands?

Nearly two thousand years ago, a man who had been born a slave built an entire philosophy around exactly this question. His answer is surprisingly short. And if you take it seriously, it can change the way you meet almost every difficulty in your life.

sections.heading: The Slave Who Became a Teacher
sections.text:
His name was Epictetus. He was born around the year 50, in Hierapolis, a city in what is today western Turkey. He grew up as the property of another man, Epaphroditus, a powerful freedman at the court of the emperor Nero. Ancient sources tell us that Epictetus was lame, and some say his master was the cause.

Think about what that means. For years, Epictetus did not own his time, his work, or even his body. Almost everything that people usually rely on to feel secure was simply not his.

At some point he was freed, and he studied philosophy with the Stoic teacher Musonius Rufus. When the emperor Domitian banished the philosophers from Rome, Epictetus moved to Nicopolis, in Greece. There he opened a school. Students travelled from far away to hear him, and one of them, Arrian, wrote down his lectures. Those notes are the reason we can still read Epictetus today.

His teaching was not written for scholars. It was meant for people who wanted to live better. And it begins with a single distinction.

sections.heading: The Dichotomy of Control

quote.lead: The first lines of his Handbook, the Enchiridion, read like this.
quote.text: Some things are in our control and others not. Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions.
quote.author: Epictetus, Enchiridion 1

sections.text:
Notice what is on that list. Your judgments. Your intentions. What you choose to pursue, and what you choose to avoid. These belong to you.

And then there is the other list. Your body, your possessions, your reputation, your position in the world. Epictetus says these are not fully up to us. That does not mean they are unimportant. It means that they depend, at least in part, on things outside of us: on other people, on chance, on time, on illness and luck.

This is not a cold idea. It is an honest one. The traffic is not up to you. Whether your boss is in a good mood is not up to you. Whether the people you love will stay healthy is, in the end, not up to you. You can influence many of these things, and you should. But you cannot command them.

What you can command is how you respond. And Epictetus believed that much of our suffering comes from mixing up the two lists. We treat the things outside our control as if they should obey us, and then we feel betrayed when they don't.

sections.heading: Not the Things Themselves

quote.lead: In the fifth chapter of the Handbook, he puts it even more sharply.
quote.text: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.
quote.author: Epictetus, Enchiridion 5

sections.text:
Of course, this does not mean that pain is imaginary, or that losing a job or a person is nothing. Epictetus was not asking us to pretend.

He was pointing at something subtler. Between an event and our reaction, there is a judgment. The car in front of you is slow. That is the event. "This is a disaster, my whole day is ruined." That is the judgment. And it is the judgment that sets your heart racing.

This idea turned out to be remarkably durable. In the twentieth century, the psychologist Albert Ellis named Epictetus as an inspiration for his rational emotive behavior therapy. Aaron Beck, the founder of cognitive therapy, also traced the philosophical origins of his approach back to the Stoics. The core insight of these therapies is close to what Epictetus taught. Our interpretations shape our emotions. And interpretations can be examined, questioned, and changed.

sections.heading: The Archer
sections.text:
But wait, you might say. If only my own judgments are fully up to me, should I stop caring about results? Should I stop trying to get the job, to win the match, to help the people I love?

The Stoics had an answer to this, and it is one of their most beautiful images. The Roman writer Cicero describes it in his work On Ends. Imagine an archer. Everything up to the moment the arrow leaves the bow is the archer's work. The training. The choice of the arrow. The stance, the aim, the calm release. After that, the wind takes over. A gust can push the arrow aside. The target can move.

A good archer does everything to hit the target. But the archer's real goal, the Stoics would say, is to shoot well. Hitting the target is something to prefer, not something to stake your peace of mind on.

The modern philosopher William Irvine suggests a practical version of this. Instead of making "win the tennis match" your goal, make your goal "play as well as I can." The first depends on your opponent. The second depends on you. And often, people who think this way perform better, because they are no longer distracted by fear of an outcome they cannot command.

sections.heading: The World of Epictetus
sections.text:
In 1965, the American pilot James Stockdale was shot down over North Vietnam. As he floated down on his parachute, he later wrote, he whispered to himself that he was leaving the world of technology and entering the world of Epictetus.

He spent more than seven years as a prisoner of war, much of it in brutal conditions. Stockdale had studied Epictetus at university, and he later said that the Handbook helped him endure. He could not control his captivity. He could control whether he kept his integrity, and how he treated the men imprisoned with him.

Most of us will never face anything like that. But the same distinction is available to us in small, ordinary moments. In an argument. In a hospital waiting room. In the middle of the night, when worries arrive one after another.

sections.heading: A Practice for Today
sections.text:
So how do you actually use this? Here is a simple exercise, in the spirit of the Handbook.

The next time something upsets you, pause, and divide the situation into two columns. In the first column, write down what is outside your control. Other people's words. The weather. The past. The outcome. In the second column, write down what is still yours. Your next action. Your tone of voice. How you interpret what happened. What you choose to let go of.

Then do something surprising. Spend your energy only on the second column. Not because the first column doesn't matter, but because you cannot change it by worrying about it.

Over time, this becomes less of an exercise and more of a way of seeing. You begin to notice how much of your stress comes from trying to hold things that were never in your hands. And you begin to notice how much freedom there is in the small space that remains.

Epictetus had very little. No freedom for much of his life. A body that caused him pain. No wealth worth mentioning. And yet he became one of the freest thinkers of the ancient world. Not because the world obeyed him, but because he stopped demanding that it should.

So the next time you find yourself stuck in traffic, try asking his question. What here is truly mine? The answer may be smaller than you hoped. And far more powerful than you think.

short.title: The one question that freed a slave
short.text:
Epictetus was born a slave. For years, he did not own his time, his work, or even his body. And yet he became one of the freest thinkers of the ancient world.

His secret was a single distinction. Some things are in our control, and some are not. Other people's opinions, the past, the outcome. Not yours. Your judgment, your next action, how you respond. Yours.

Much of our suffering, he believed, comes from mixing up the two. We demand that the world obey us, and feel betrayed when it doesn't.

So the next time something upsets you, ask his question. What here is truly mine? Then spend your energy only there.
